name: Lena Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. We do not sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach cello in the morning, arrange a few bars for a client after lunch, and rehearse with my quartet when everyone is free. I have a master’s in music and can hear a bad bow stroke across the room, but keeping enough paid hours together is the hard part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part keeps you coming back, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A student finally finding a clean note is lovely. Chasing a late venue payment when the rent is due wears me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the quartet that a better booking form is hardly a new orchestra. We still have to tune, listen and get people into a room together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet winter already frightens me more than a clever form. I have three weeks of rent in the bank, and one cancelled wedding puts me behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep the Thursday teaching slots and the Saturday quartet dates this winter. If the bookings hold, I will put a little from each performance into a rent envelope, though some months there is no little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tired rather than surprised. My cello does not pay the electricity bill until somebody hires me to play it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if one Saturday booking disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Saturday wedding falls through, the electricity bill waits until the next lesson fees come in. I have done that once and I hated opening the envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a student about the routine tasks AI can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my students that a machine can print a neat part but cannot hear where their bow shakes. That is the bit I can teach.

say: I would tell the **quartet** that booking forms may improve, while live playing still needs us.
I would say my **students** still need a teacher who hears their hands.
think: I have only **three weeks** of rent saved, so even an ordinary cancellation can hurt.
I worry more about the **quiet winter** than the software on its own.
do: Keep my **Thursday lessons** and Saturday quartet dates through the winter.
Put any spare **performance pay** into a rent envelope after the bills clear.
feel: I feel **tired** because the same money worry stays with me.
S0.quote: My cello does not pay the electricity bill until somebody hires me to play it.
fieldNote: Her public **confidence** in live music sits beside a fragile rent position.
The one cancelled **wedding** she describes is a real income shock, even with little AI change.

steps.text: Keep Thursday cello lessons and Saturday quartet bookings
Put spare performance pay into a rent envelope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say at rehearsal that venues will use software for posters, schedules and cheap backing tracks. I would ask our players to talk together before a venue changes the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I privately think my recording arrangements will go first, because a client can ask a machine for ten versions overnight. Lessons might last longer, but parents may start questioning the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask the local musicians association for its model contract and take it to our quartet. In the first year of this shift, I would keep direct lesson calls and ask each venue for a written live fee before holding a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious. A smaller arrangement fee leaves no soft landing between teaching terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work would the software touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cafe owner on Market Street already asks me to arrange a short tune for every opening night. I would stop treating those one-off fees as money I can count on for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can other musicians do together if a venue cuts its fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can ask other players to insist on a fee, but I cannot force a venue to hire us. I would want the association at the table with the bigger bookers.

say: I would tell the **quartet** that schedules and backing tracks may become cheap.
I would ask players to press for a **written live fee** together.
think: My **recording arrangements** could disappear before the teaching and live dates.
A lower **lesson price** would squeeze me between teaching terms.
do: Ask the **musicians association** for its model contract this month.
Get a **written fee** from venues before holding each live date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing the small fees that pay rent between terms.
S1.quote: A smaller arrangement fee leaves no soft landing between teaching terms.
fieldNote: Her **arrangement income** is exposed to thinking AI before robots matter to live performance.
Her association plan is **collective**, but she knows a contract cannot create bookings.

steps.text: Ask the musicians association for its model live contract
Keep direct calls with cello students each term
Get written live fees before holding venue dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the quartet that by 2028 a machine may write the score and plan the whole tour. I would say live people still deserve a wage, and we should refuse free trial performances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alone, I think my arranging income would vanish in 2028, before any 2031 robot could carry a cello onstage. I cannot pay rent for three years on a theory that audiences will always choose us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I would ask our association about an emergency fund and bring my last six invoices. If AGI arrives in 2028, I would apply for income help immediately and cut the rented studio hour before I touch my home rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed, though I would still have lessons and concerts to chase. The short clock makes every rehearsal feel borrowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which payment would you cut first, and how much is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio costs me 90 a month, which is about two private lessons. I would record in my bedroom, even though the sound there is poor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want the quartet to hold together; what can you promise them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the quartet to agree on minimum fees, but I cannot promise them the same number of concerts. I am not ready to move to a city on a maybe.

say: I would tell the **quartet** that machine scores do not justify unpaid live trials.
I would argue for **minimum fees** before venues change terms.
think: My **arranging income** may vanish in 2028, while hands-on stage work faces robots around 2031.
Three years of live work would not guarantee **rent** if bookings thin out.
do: Bring six **invoices** to the association and ask about emergency help tomorrow.
Cancel the **studio hour** at 90 monthly if AGI removes arranging fees in 2028.
Apply for **income help** in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the short clock and my nearly empty savings.
S2.quote: I cannot pay rent for three years on a theory that audiences will always choose us.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 score threat** from the later 2031 robot threat.
Her first cut is a **studio hour**, preserving housing and her ability to teach.

steps.text: Ask association about help now; apply in first year after 2028 AGI
Cancel the 90 monthly studio hour if 2028 AGI removes arranging fees
Agree minimum live fees with the quartet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell students that AGI by 2031 gives us a few seasons to decide what a human lesson is worth. I would still push venues to name the musician and pay for the performance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, five years would let me build a class that returns each term. I still expect automated arrangements by 2031, and by around 2034 robots might copy more stage work, though I do not know whether audiences would buy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I would add a small group cello class at the library if the room is free. By 2031 I would aim for a regular list of twelve pupils, and in the first year after AGI I would keep the classes while dropping cheap arrangement commissions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be anxious, but I could see a calendar rather than a cliff. Five years would let me find out whether families come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many pupils would make the group class useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve pupils would cover the rent only if at least ten pay each month. I would count paid places, not names on a sign-up sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to run those lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not want to call a machine my co-teacher. I would rather teach small groups and keep the price low enough that a child can stay.

say: I would tell families that **human lessons** need fair fees and regular places.
I would ask venues to **name and pay** the players they book.
think: Five years might let me build a **returning class** before arrangements dry up.
I cannot assume families will pay for **human lessons** when machine music is cheap.
do: Start a **group cello class** at the library next term if the room is free.
Count **paid pupils** each month and keep the class after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years gives me a usable calendar.
S3.quote: I would count paid places, not names on a sign-up sheet.
fieldNote: She treats the extra **five years** as time to test recurring teaching revenue.
Her refusal to use AI is consistent with **resistance**, while group teaching is a familiar change.

steps.text: Start a paid library cello group if the room is free
Keep teaching returning pupils after 2031 AGI arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my students that AGI by 2036 gives us ten years of lessons and concerts before the thinking work changes. I would ask them to keep playing together, whatever records get made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could build enough steady pupils by 2036 to lose the arranging work without losing the flat. Robots might reach the stage around 2039, but the question then is whether anyone still pays for the room and the people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would put one lesson fee each month into a separate account when the month allows. Before 2036 I would try to build my library class to two groups, then use the first year after AGI to keep teaching and judge live bookings month by month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about this winter, even though ten years gives me time to build a living less dependent on one-off scores. I cannot pay the next rent bill with a future plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you really save a lesson fee every month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could not promise one fee every month this winter. If the quartet has a good month, I would save then and not pretend the amount is regular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a student to carry into that future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A violinist can lose the page of music and still know the tune. I want students to learn that sort of courage, not just a better file.

say: I would tell students to keep **playing together** through the decade.
I would ask venues to pay for **people in the room**.
think: Ten years might make my **teaching income** sturdy enough to lose arranging fees.
I remain unsure whether **2039 stage robots** would change what audiences buy.
do: Save one **lesson fee** in good months starting this year.
Grow the **library cello class** toward two groups before 2036.
feel: I feel **anxious** about this winter, though the longer clock gives me time to build teaching.
S4.quote: A violinist can lose the page of music and still know the tune.
fieldNote: She sees the **decade** as a chance to shift income toward repeat pupils.
Her savings plan stays **conditional** on the few months when fees actually arrive, leaving current rent pressure intact.

steps.text: Save one lesson fee in months with spare cash
Grow the library cello class toward two paid groups
Judge live quartet bookings month by month after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the arranging fees could go before I have a cushion. A real emergency payment and a fair live contract would give me time to keep teaching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid for the music a machine learned from. My students and the quartet cannot live on applause, even when a room is full.

headlineQuote: My students and the quartet cannot live on applause, even when a room is full.
portrait: At **27**, Lena is a skilled cellist with a music master’s degree who teaches, arranges and plays in a quartet.
Her **thin savings** make even AI Plateau anxious because a cancelled performance can disturb rent and bills.
She resists **AI tools** and asks musicians to bargain together over live fees as arrangements become cheaper.
A **five or ten year** runway lets her test group teaching and save only when paid work permits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase arrangement fees before Lena builds a rent cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Emergency income help** and a fair live contract would let Lena keep teaching through the first shock.
